sentences.text: It is a well-settled proposition of law that the essential requirement for proving an offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC is the existence of the dishonest or fraudulent intention of the accused at the very moment the inducement was made.
This indispensable mental element, or mens-rea, must be antecedent to the commission of the act of deception and subsequent delivery of property.
A mere subsequent failure to fulfil a promise or a breach of contractual obligation does not automatically translate into a criminal offence under Section 420.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Hridaya Ranjan Prasad Verma v. State of Bihar (2000) 4 SCC 168), unequivocally distinguished between civil liability and criminal culpability, holding:

It is necessary that the complainant should place material before the Court to satisfy that the accused had the fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise."

25. Further building upon the requirement of initial intention, apex Court has repeatedly emphasized that the courts must scrupulously examine whether the material on record demonstrates the accused's deceptive intent at the time of the transaction.
The ingredients of Section 415 must be strictly satisfied.
If the intention to cheat developed only after the property was delivered, the offence of cheating is not made out.

In the case of Deepak Gaba and Ors. v. State of U.P and Anr. (2024) SCC OnLine SC 316), it was reaffirmed that the core of the offence lies in the deception and not merely the loss of property, observing:
"The test to be applied is whether the conduct of the accused was capable of giving rise to an inference that he entertained an intention to cheat at the initial stage itself.
Mere breach of contract, even if accompanied by non-payment, cannot be the foundation for a criminal prosecution for cheating."

The essence of the offence of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC is the agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act.

The punishment for criminal conspiracy is invoked upon the establishment of this 'meeting of minds,'
which need not be formally recorded but can be inferred from surrounding circumstances.

The landmark ruling in Kehar Singh v. State (Delhi Administration)
(1988) 3 SCC 609) remains the cornerstone for defining this offence, stating:
"The conspiracy is an agreement to do an illegal act or to do a legal act by illegal means.

sentences.text: The offence of conspiracy is complete the moment two or more persons agree to do an illegal act.
It is not necessary that the object of the agreement should be achieved."

27. Therefore, for the combined charge of Section 420 read with Section 120B IPC, the prosecution must prove an agreement to perpetrate the fraud, followed by the commission of acts of cheating pursuant to that agreement.
Further, given the clandestine nature of conspiracy, direct evidence of the agreement is rarely obtainable.
Consequently, the proof must often rely upon circumstantial evidence and the reasonable inferences deducible from the common intention of the parties.
The apex Court permits the inference of conspiracy from the facts and circumstances of the case, the conduct of the parties, and the overt acts committed by them towards the common object.

The crucial legal requirement is the demonstration of a prior consensus and a concerted plan to dishonestly induce the delivery of property, thereby linking the offence of cheating to the criminal design under the ambit of Section 120B IPC.

The essence of the offence of criminal conspiracy under Section 120B IPC is the agreement between two or more persons to commit an illegal act.
The punishment for criminal conspiracy is invoked upon the establishment of this 'meeting of minds,'
which need not be formally recorded but can be inferred from surrounding circumstances.
The offence of conspiracy is complete the moment two or more persons agree to do an illegal act.
It is not necessary that the object of the agreement should be achieved."
